This note tests four quarters of management's story (fiscal Q4 2025 through fiscal Q3 2026) against the hard numbers our screener pulled.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has been remarkably consistent quarter to quarter — and that consistency is itself a data point. Across all four calls the refrain is identical: "AI is changing everything and you can't run AI without Arm" (Q4 FY25), narrowing to "from milliwatts to megawatts" and, by the latest call, "from milliwatts to gigawatts." The core claim never wavers: Arm is the one compute platform that spans the smallest battery device to the largest hyperscale data center.

What *did* evolve is where the growth is coming from. Early calls leaned on smartphones (royalties up 30% year-on-year in Q4 FY25 "far outpacing the modest 2% growth in shipments"). By the most recent call (fiscal Q3 2026, reported February 2026) the emphasis has decisively shifted to the data center: "our data center royalty revenue has grown more than 100% year on year, and we expect in a few years our data center business to be our largest business, larger than mobile." Compute Subsystems (CSS) — pre-integrated bundles that carry Arm's highest royalty rates — went from a talking point to the central royalty engine, climbing from 13 licenses to 21 across the four quarters.

The single most important new thread, and it appears only *after* our transcript window closes, is Arm building its own physical chip — the Arm AGI CPU. The transcripts foreshadow it: management repeatedly says it is "exploring the possibility of moving beyond our current platform into additional compute subsystems, chiplets and potentially full-end solutions" (fiscal Q1 and Q2 2026), and the Lee Simpson chiplet question in Q4 FY25 probes exactly this. The story is expanding, not contracting — but it is expanding into a far more capital-intensive, lower-margin, and customer-conflicting business than the pure-licensing model the multiple was built on.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record royalty… growing value of every chip" | Royalty rose from $607M (Q4 FY25) to a record $737M (Q3 FY26), +27% YoY; full-year revenue $4.01B → $4.92B (+22.8%) | **Matches.** Royalty growth is real and broad-based. |
| Smartphone royalties "grew an order of magnitude faster than the market" | Corroborated by the mix-shift story (Armv9 + CSS raise the rate per chip); gross margin held at ~92.5% | **Matches** — the asset-light licensing model is genuinely elite. |
| Data center "grew more than 100% year on year… will be larger than mobile" | Not separately broken out in our financials, but total revenue growth (+22.8%) and the royalty acceleration (18% → 25% → 21% → 27% YoY across the four quarters) support a rising infrastructure mix | **Plausible, unverified in detail** — the segment split we were given is only Royalty 53% / License 47%, not by end-market. |
| "Accelerating investment in our R&D" | Net income is volatile and margin-thin for the multiple: FY24 net income actually *fell* to $306M (EPS $0.29) before recovering to $792M (FY25) and $904M (FY26). Net margin is just 18.4% | **Matches, and it is the tension.** Rising R&D is real and it is capping earnings. |
| Free cash flow strength | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $951M on a company the market values at roughly $330B — a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of about 344 times | **The story is far richer than the cash flow.** This is the central forensic finding. |

The narrative is honest about the business but the *price* is not honest about the cash. Revenue growing ~23% is excellent; it does not remotely support 344 times free cash flow on any conventional discounted-cash-flow math. Our own model bears this out brutally: every internal valuation method (discounted cash flow, earnings power value, Graham, owner earnings) returns a margin of safety of −100%, i.e. the stock trades at a price these methods cannot reach at all. The screener's own discounted-cash-flow fair value is $12.4 against a $315 price.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising and unwavering.** Every call opens with a superlative — "record-breaking close" (Q4 FY25), "highest revenue quarter" / "second highest" (Q1 FY26), "best second quarter ever" (Q2 FY26), "record third quarter" (Q3 FY26). CEO Rene Haas closes each call with escalating conviction: "the future has never been brighter" (Q2), "the growth trajectory of the company, I think, is unparalleled" (Q1).

There is a subtle but important shift from *offensive* to *even-more-offensive* — not toward defense. Where most companies pivot to efficiency language late-cycle, Arm is doing the opposite: it is *accelerating* spending and expanding into capital-intensive silicon at the top of an AI-capex cycle. That is confidence, but it is confidence that raises execution risk rather than lowering it. The one defensive note is repeated tariff/macro caveats ("we do not consider it prudent to issue full year guidance," Q4 FY25) — but these read as genuine prudence, not a tell.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High — score: High.** Our financials show a beat rate of 6 of 7 quarters (86%), and the transcripts corroborate a consistent pattern of landing at or above the high end. Q4 FY25 EPS of $0.55 came "at the high end of our guidance range of $0.48 to $0.56." Q2 FY26 revenue "exceeded the midpoint of our guidance range by $75 million." Royalty repeatedly beat: Q2 FY26 "growing 21% year-on-year… versus our guidance of mid-teens."

There is a mild sandbagging pattern on royalty (guides mid-teens, delivers low-to-high-20s) but it is modest and consistent, not a red flag. The one honest wobble: management withdrew full-year guidance in Q4 FY25 citing tariff uncertainty, then delivered strongly anyway — prudence that proved conservative. Guidance reliability is genuinely a green mark here.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts circled three themes repeatedly, and management's answers grew *less* specific over time on the one that matters most:

1. **Arm building its own chips (channel conflict).** Lee Simpson (Morgan Stanley) probed this directly in Q4 FY25 — "is it a waypoint perhaps to the eventual own chip-making Arm?" — and management deflected ("regarding unannounced products, I'm not going to announce anything here"). This is the deflection that later became the biggest news, and the biggest risk: competing with your own licensees.
2. **Armv9 adoption percentage.** Management *stopped disclosing* the v9 penetration number (Q1 FY26: "we're now just going to update this on an annual basis"), reframing it as potentially "misleading." Reduced disclosure on a key adoption metric is a yellow flag even when the stated reason (royalty-rate growth decoupling from unit penetration) is plausible.
3. **China concentration.** China rose to ~21–22% of revenue (Q1–Q2 FY26). Management insists it "largely tracks the global market" and export controls have limited impact — but a fifth of revenue in a geopolitically fraught market is a standing risk analysts keep testing.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Royalty acceleration is real and broad-based (data center royalties up triple digits).
🟢 Gross margin ~92.5% and stable — a genuinely elite, asset-light licensing model.
🟢 Guidance credibility high; beat 6 of 7 quarters; net cash of $3.14B (cash $3.60B vs debt $457M).
🟢 CSS drives the highest royalty rates Arm has ever seen and adoption "continues to exceed expectations."

🔴 Valuation is disconnected from cash: ~344x trailing free cash flow, every internal method at −100% margin of safety, analyst consensus target ($315.56) implies *zero* upside from here.
🔴 The vertical-integration pivot (building the Arm AGI CPU) puts Arm into direct conflict with the licensees who *are its royalty base* — a strategic risk to the very moat, not just a margin question.
🔴 Rising R&D is structurally capping net margin (18.4%) and will do so more as chip development scales; FY24 already showed how quickly net income can halve ($306M) in an investment year.
🔴 Insider behavior is one-sided: zero open-market buys against 24 sells (212,637 shares). No insider is putting new money in at this price.
🔴 Reduced disclosure on Armv9 penetration.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling terminology shift is the widening of the tagline from "milliwatts to megawatts" (fiscal Q1/Q2 2026) to "milliwatts to **gigawatts**" (fiscal Q3 2026). That is not idle marketing — it signals management repositioning Arm as central to the very largest AI build-outs, the ground on which it will now compete with its own customers via the AGI CPU.

The reorganization into three business units — Edge AI, Physical AI, Cloud AI (announced Q3 FY26) — is a structural tell that management is preparing to run a more product-like, less pure-IP business. Combined with the repeated "chiplets… potentially full-end solutions" language and the expanded SoftBank relationship ("build towards their greater, broader AI vision"), the signal is clear: Arm is becoming something other than the frictionless royalty machine the multiple assumes. Whether that is value-accretive or margin-dilutive is the whole debate.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING on fundamentals, but the business model is PIVOTING** from pure licensing toward capital-intensive own-silicon. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a truly excellent business priced for a decade of flawless execution, and the pivot that could justify the price is the same pivot that threatens the moat.** You are not underwriting whether Arm is a good company (it is); you are underwriting whether ~344x free cash flow can be grown into — and doing so *while* Arm picks a fight with the licensees who pay its royalties.

**Moat:** WIDE but with the trend under question. The economic moat is intangible-asset and switching-cost based — the Arm instruction set is the de-facto standard, over 22 million developers build on it (>80% of the world's base), and Kleidi AI has 8 billion-plus installs. Returns tell a more cautious story: return on invested capital is only ~8.0% and return on equity ~11.3% — *below* what a 92% gross-margin franchise "should" earn, because heavy R&D reinvestment is depressing the denominator's payoff today. That is a widening-investment moat if the AGI CPU works, and a self-inflicted eroding one if own-silicon alienates licensees. On balance the moat is wide and durable in its core licensing form; I mark it WIDE / STABLE, with an explicit warning that the pivot is the swing factor.

**Secular force:** Arm is a *beneficiary* of the AI-compute wave, not a victim of a secular decline. There is no cord-cutting, disintermediation, or reimbursement-compression tail impairing terminal value. The real risk is not secular decline but cyclical/positioning: a rich AI name in a de-grossing tape. Cheapness is *not* the question here — the stock is the opposite of cheap. This is a quality-priced-for-perfection setup, not a value trap and not a fear-print.

🔴 The vertical-integration pivot (building the Arm AGI CPU) puts Arm into direct conflict with the licensees who *are its royalty base* — a strategic risk to the very moat, not just a margin question.
🔴 Rising R&D is structurally capping net margin (18.4%) and will do so more as chip development scales; FY24 already showed how quickly net income can halve ($306M) in an investment year.
🔴 Insider behavior is one-sided: zero open-market buys against 24 sells (212,637 shares). No insider is putting new money in at this price.
🔴 Reduced disclosure on Armv9 penetration.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling terminology shift is the widening of the tagline from "milliwatts to megawatts" (fiscal Q1/Q2 2026) to "milliwatts to **gigawatts**" (fiscal Q3 2026). That is not idle marketing — it signals management repositioning Arm as central to the very largest AI build-outs, the ground on which it will now compete with its own customers via the AGI CPU.

The reorganization into three business units — Edge AI, Physical AI, Cloud AI (announced Q3 FY26) — is a structural tell that management is preparing to run a more product-like, less pure-IP business. Combined with the repeated "chiplets… potentially full-end solutions" language and the expanded SoftBank relationship ("build towards their greater, broader AI vision"), the signal is clear: Arm is becoming something other than the frictionless royalty machine the multiple assumes. Whether that is value-accretive or margin-dilutive is the whole debate.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING on fundamentals, but the business model is PIVOTING** from pure licensing toward capital-intensive own-silicon. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a truly excellent business priced for a decade of flawless execution, and the pivot that could justify the price is the same pivot that threatens the moat.** You are not underwriting whether Arm is a good company (it is); you are underwriting whether ~344x free cash flow can be grown into — and doing so *while* Arm picks a fight with the licensees who pay its royalties.

**Moat:** WIDE but with the trend under question. The economic moat is intangible-asset and switching-cost based — the Arm instruction set is the de-facto standard, over 22 million developers build on it (>80% of the world's base), and Kleidi AI has 8 billion-plus installs. Returns tell a more cautious story: return on invested capital is only ~8.0% and return on equity ~11.3% — *below* what a 92% gross-margin franchise "should" earn, because heavy R&D reinvestment is depressing the denominator's payoff today. That is a widening-investment moat if the AGI CPU works, and a self-inflicted eroding one if own-silicon alienates licensees. On balance the moat is wide and durable in its core licensing form; I mark it WIDE / STABLE, with an explicit warning that the pivot is the swing factor.

**Secular force:** Arm is a *beneficiary* of the AI-compute wave, not a victim of a secular decline. There is no cord-cutting, disintermediation, or reimbursement-compression tail impairing terminal value. The real risk is not secular decline but cyclical/positioning: a rich AI name in a de-grossing tape. Cheapness is *not* the question here — the stock is the opposite of cheap. This is a quality-priced-for-perfection setup, not a value trap and not a fear-print.

bull_thesis:
Arm collects a toll on the world's computing. Its designs sit inside roughly 350 billion chips shipped to date, and about 22 million software developers - some 80% of the world's total - build on top of them. That is a genuinely rare asset, and the operating record backs it up: revenue grew 23% in the fiscal year ended March 2026 to $4.92B, the third straight year above 20%, with a 92.5% gross margin (the share of revenue left after the direct cost of delivering it), $3.14B of net cash and no solvency question whatsoever.

The bullish case has three legs. First, Arm is paid more for every chip, every year. Royalties from smartphones have been growing 'an order of magnitude faster than the market' (management, quarter ended September 2025) while the number of phones sold barely grows at all - because each new generation of Arm's architecture carries a higher rate than the last. Management was explicit in the quarter ended June 2025 that 'each generation of v9 is higher than the previous one,' so the rate rises even without new customers. Pricing power that compounds against flat unit volumes is the signature of a strengthening franchise, not a fading one.

Second, the data centre. Arm's share at the largest cloud providers is around 50%, its designs sit in essentially every major custom server chip (Amazon's Graviton, Google's Axion, Microsoft's Cobalt, Nvidia's Grace and Vera), and it holds close to 100% share in the networking chips that shuffle data around those buildings. Data-centre royalties have more than doubled year-on-year for several quarters running. Management expects this to become its largest business.

Third, and this is what re-rated the stock, Arm now sells its own chip. The Arm AGI CPU, announced with results in May 2026 and co-developed with Meta as lead partner, already carries 'more than $2 billion of customer demand across fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028 - more than double what we stated at launch,' pointing toward a $15B revenue target by fiscal 2031 alongside an intellectual-property business management expects to double to $10B. If both land, Arm earns roughly $8-11 per share by 2031 against $1.77 last year.

The conditions this depends on are precise: the artificial-intelligence build-out must keep spending at current pace; Arm must secure the manufacturing capacity to actually ship the AGI chip; and the market must keep paying a premium multiple for a revenue base that is deliberately mixing toward lower-margin hardware.
bear_thesis:
The bearish case does not argue that Arm is a bad business. It is an excellent business. The case is that the annuity is decelerating, the growth carrying the story is partly not what it appears, and the price already assumes the five-year plan works perfectly.

Start with the number that matters most. Royalties - the recurring, near-costless per-chip toll that is the real asset - grew 27% in the quarter ended December 2025 and then just 11% in the quarter ended March 2026. Growth more than halved in a single quarter, and royalties fell $66M sequentially, from $737M to $671M. Seasonality explains the sequential dip; it does not explain a growth rate collapsing from 27 to 11 against a year-ago comparison. This also punctures the most-quoted bullish statistic: management sized cloud and networking at 'around 10-ish percent' of royalties trending to '15% to 20%' (quarter ended September 2025), so the data centre is doubling roughly a sixth of royalties while the other ~80% decelerates underneath. Doubling a sixth and stalling the rest produces exactly the 11% that printed. The bull's best fact and the bear's best fact are the same fact.

Second, the licensing line that carried the year is partly self-dealt. Reported licensing rose 29% to $819M in the quarter ended March 2026. In the same breath the finance chief disclosed that '$200 million' of it came from 'our agreement with SoftBank for technology licensing and design services... flat with the prior quarter.' SoftBank owns about 87% of Arm. So roughly 24% of that quarter's licensing was billed to Arm's own parent, at an $800M annual run-rate against a $2.31B licensing business, and at least $400M of the fiscal-2026 licensing total is disclosed related-party revenue. Strip the $200M out and third-party licensing was $619M against $634M in the year-ago quarter - flat to slightly down, versus the reported +29%. (The year-ago figure may contain its own undisclosed SoftBank amount, so read this as indicative rather than exact.) Revenue from your controlling shareholder is not market demand and cannot be extrapolated - particularly while that same shareholder's founder publicly floats a '$4 trillion' valuation for the asset he controls (widely reported 24 June 2026).

Third, and most damaging: Arm's own finance chief has refused to underwrite the growth rate the market is capitalising, on four consecutive calls. Against reported contract-value growth of 22-28%, he has repeatedly named the structural rate as 'mid to high single digit,' most recently 'high single-digit, low double-digit range... at least 10% year-on-year growth for the long term is probably the floor' (quarter ended March 2026). He even names the cause - 'this kind of AI investment super cycle or whatever folks are calling it... who knows how much longer it goes.' The company guides ~10%; consensus models 22-28%.

Fourth, the mix shift destroys the model's quality even as it grows the top line. The AGI silicon business underpinning the $15B target runs at about 30-35% gross margin and roughly a 35% operating margin, against 65% for the intellectual-property business - management's own figures. Growing from $4.9B at 92.5% gross margin to $25B at a blended margin far below that is more revenue and a structurally worse business. The market applies a licensor's multiple to a base that is mixing toward hardware.

Fifth, management pre-flagged the problem the market has only just found. On 6 May 2026 the finance chief hedged the AGI ramp himself: 'let's just assume that's the number until we work through some of the wafer and memory shortage issues.' On 14 July 2026 HSBC downgraded Arm to Hold on exactly that thesis - foundry capacity bottlenecks capping earnings upside - and BofA the same day flagged near-term pain for Arm while favouring AMD.

Sixth, revealed behaviour contradicts stated confidence: zero open-market insider purchases against 24 sales (212,637 shares) through a roughly 330% advance. Not one insider bought.

What confirms the bear: royalty growth staying at or below the low teens on 29 July; any softening of the '$2 billion' AGI demand figure; or a cloud-provider capital-spending guide-down in late July. At about 293 times trailing free cash flow, roughly 148 times last year's adjusted earnings and about 56 times enterprise value to sales, none of this needs to go badly wrong for the stock to fall - it only needs to go merely well.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about whether Arm is a great business - it is - but about three things the street has mis-read.

First, and most concretely: the analyst price targets are a lagging record of the share price, not a forecast of it, and our own screener is reading them backwards. The screener flags 'analyst-target velocity +46%' as a bullish signal. Look at what actually produced that number. The three targets set in the last month average $428.33; the 19 set over the last year average $262.63. The street more than doubled its targets as the stock went parabolic. Second, consensus capitalises a licensing growth rate that Arm's own finance chief has disowned four times. The street models the 22-28% contract-value growth as structural. Management has said, on four consecutive calls, that the real rate is 'mid to high single digit' and most recently that 'at least 10% year-on-year growth for the long term is probably the floor,' while naming the cause as an artificial-intelligence investment super-cycle whose duration 'who knows.' When a finance chief repeatedly refuses to underwrite his own reported growth, the burden of proof sits with the extrapolation, not the caution.

Third - and this one appears to be genuinely unpriced - nobody has discounted the mix shift or the related-party revenue. The $15B of fiscal-2031 silicon revenue that justifies the multiple runs at roughly 30-35% gross margin against an intellectual-property business at 92.5%; the market is paying a licensor's multiple for a base deliberately mixing toward hardware. And roughly 24% of the licensing quarter that carried the year ($200M of $819M) was billed to Arm's ~87% owner, at an $800M annual run-rate. This was disclosed unprompted on 6 May 2026 and drew not one analyst follow-up. Two of the four biggest quality-of-earnings issues in this business have never been asked about on a call.

Where we do NOT disagree with the market: the moat. Arm's franchise is wide and widening, and any bear arguing erosion is arguing the wrong thing. Our disagreement is entirely about price.
forcing_function:

The nearer and more powerful is the cloud providers' second-quarter results in late July, Alphabet first at roughly 22-28 July 2026. The second is Arm's own Q1 fiscal-2027 report on 29 July 2026 after the close (confirmed by Business Wire, 8 July 2026), with a call at 5pm Eastern. To justify $262 the company must beat a five-year plan it has already hedged; to break the price it need only report the sequentially-down quarter consensus already expects, in a tape that just punished TSMC for a blowout. valley_of_death:
The risky window is unusually short and unusually well-defined: the next two weeks.

There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall - Arm has $3.14B of net cash, $457M of total debt and an Altman-Z solvency score of 81. Nothing here threatens the company. What threatens the shares is an optically ugly quarter that is already contractually scheduled.

positioning_washout:
This is the most interesting structural feature of the name, and it argues for patience rather than purchase.

The shareholder base is nothing like the yield-focused or passive base this question usually contemplates. SoftBank owns roughly 87% of Arm, so the free float - the shares actually available to trade - is only about 13%, roughly 138M shares or about $36B against a $278.8B market capitalisation. That tiny float is the mechanical key to the whole chart. It is why the stock could triple from about $105 in January to $452.70 in June on relatively modest inflows, and it is why it can fall 42% in four weeks on modest outflows. A thin float amplifies violently in both directions and offers no support on the way down.

Who holds that float is momentum money, not value money. Arm sits in every artificial-intelligence and semiconductor index and momentum basket. Leveraged single-stock exchange-traded funds tied to chip and artificial-intelligence winners were up over 500% in the first half of 2026 - those vehicles rebalance daily and mechanically sell into declines, converting a drawdown into an accelerant. Stanley Druckenmiller's Duquesne disclosed a position in the first-quarter 2026 filing (15 May 2026) - fast money, not patient capital. After a 42% drawdown, momentum-factor rebalancing will mechanically eject the name from the very baskets that bid it up, and that selling is price-insensitive.

So the forced selling is real, it is happening right now, and - this is the point - it is NOT finished. Momentum unwinds overshoot, and a 13% float means the overshoot can be far more violent than the fundamentals justify. There is no natural buyer underneath: no dividend to attract income holders, no valuation support (the stock is roughly 40% above our own base fair value even after the fall), no activist angle (SoftBank's 87% makes any governance campaign structurally impossible), and no buyback of consequence. The one holder who could support the stock, SoftBank, is also the one selling Arm's story to the public while collecting $200M a quarter from it.

The honest conclusion: the wash-out is in progress, not complete, and there is no floor mechanic to catch it. That is a reason to wait, not a reason to step in.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now - and to be clear about why, this is a pass on price, not on quality.

Arm is one of the best businesses in this universe. The moat is wide and genuinely widening: it is paid more per chip every single generation while phone volumes barely grow, it holds about 50% share at the largest cloud providers and close to 100% in data-centre networking chips, and roughly 22 million developers - about 80% of the world's total - are locked into its architecture by decades of compiled software. Its 92.5% gross margin has not moved, it has $3.14B of net cash, and it has now grown above 20% for three consecutive years. Management is credible: they guide conservatively, they clear their own bars, and their finance chief volunteers inconvenient facts nobody asked for. I want to be unambiguous that any bear case built on the franchise eroding is simply wrong and will lose money.

The problem is that you are being asked to pay $262.01 for about $185 of value, and the gap is not subtle. At today's price the market pays roughly $275.6B of enterprise value - about 56 times revenue, 148 times last year's adjusted earnings and 293 times trailing free cash flow. Run it the other way and the arithmetic is cleaner still: $262 is almost exactly what management's full five-year plan produces if executed flawlessly at a rich 45x exit discounted at 10%. The price already contains the plan working. You are not buying growth; you are buying the successful completion of a plan, with no margin of safety and no compensation for the plan slipping.

And the plan is already slipping in the disclosed numbers. Royalty growth - the annuity everything rests on - halved from 27% to 11% in one quarter, with royalties down $66M sequentially. The data-centre doubling everyone quotes is doubling a sixth of royalties while the other 80% decelerates; that is how you print 11%. The licensing line that carried the year is partly self-dealt: $200M of the $819M quarter was billed to SoftBank, Arm's ~87% owner, at an $800M annual run-rate, and stripping it out leaves third-party licensing flat to down against a reported +29%. The finance chief has told the street four times that the structural licensing rate is ~10%, not the 22-28% consensus capitalises. The $15B silicon business justifying the multiple runs at 30-35% gross margin against 92.5% for the intellectual property - more revenue, worse business, unpriced. And not one insider bought a share on the open market through a 330% advance while 24 sold.

On timing, the regime settles it. The market regime read names artificial-intelligence capital spending as the single dominant shared factor capable of swamping everything, flags it as a partially-breached tripwire, and names late-July results as the decision point - explicitly instructing us to prize independence from exactly this factor. Arm is the purest listed expression of it. The evidence has only worsened since that read: a $1.3T semiconductor drawdown in late June, chips sold off on 16 July despite TSMC's blowout, HSBC downgrading on 14 July on the foundry bottleneck management itself had already flagged, and the stock down 5.4% on the day to 42% below its June record. The cloud providers guide before Arm reports, so Arm carries the sector's risk without controlling its own timing. The regime does not reward this setup; it penalises it.

The catalyst deserves one plain sentence: it already fired. The move from about $105 in January to $452.70 in June was the re-rating, and it is now unwinding. The 29 July report is a hard date, but a scheduled quarterly release is not an asymmetric opportunity - it is a two-sided risk event that resolves against the price more easily than for it, since beating a hedged five-year plan is harder than printing the down quarter consensus already expects.

On the two scores landing at the same number: that is deliberate, not a default. They are reasoned separately and genuinely converge. With the catalyst and regime included, the re-rating is spent and the setup is hostile. Strip both away and ask only whether this is good value against the $185 sum-of-the-parts, and the answer is still no - you are paying about 1.4 times fair value, with roughly 16% of revenue coming from the controlling shareholder. The moat is wide and widening and the secular threat is manageable, so no quality cap binds here; this is not a value trap and I am not calling it one. It is the rarer third case - an outstanding franchise at an indefensible entry price - and both axes independently say the same thing.

What would change my mind, specifically: this becomes genuinely interesting near $185 and compelling nearer $150, but only alongside evidence the annuity is intact - royalty growth back above 20%, the AGI demand figure holding or rising with manufacturing capacity secured, and a full-year guide issued rather than withheld. Note that even at $185 you would be paying roughly 75 times forward earnings, which is why this can never be a large position. Watch it, want it, and let the forced selling finish - a 13% float with no valuation support and no floor mechanic does not stop where fair value says it should.

interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Arm Holdings plc (ARM)
**Interrogator | 2026-07-17 | Live price $262.01 (NASDAQ, USD), down 5.4% on the day, ~42% below the $452.70 record set in June 2026**

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across five consecutive calls (May 2025 → May 2026) the story did not merely grow — it changed category, and that change is the single most important thing in this file.

**May 2025 (Q4 FY25): "we license, others build."** Arm was a pure intellectual-property licensor. The pitch was royalty per chip rising as customers moved from the older v8 architecture to Armv9, plus compute subsystems (CSS — a pre-integrated bundle of Arm's own designs that customers drop into their chip, sold at a higher royalty rate than licensing the pieces separately). Rene Haas closed with "AI is changing everything and you can't run AI without Arm." Thirteen CSS licences existed. No chips of Arm's own.

**July 2025 → November 2025: the tell.** Twice, in near-identical language, management floated a strategy change without committing to it — "we are continuing to explore the possibility of moving beyond our current platform into additional compute subsystems, chiplets and potentially full-end solutions" (Q1 FY26), repeated in Q2 FY26 as "chiplets or complete SoCs." Both times the sentence's function was to pre-justify a large increase in research spending. Operating expenses went from $566M (Q4 FY25) to $619M, then $648M — up 31% year-on-year while revenue grew 34%. Note the sequencing: management booked the cost of the pivot two-to-three quarters before naming it.

**February 2026 (Q3 FY26): reorganisation.** The company re-cut itself into Edge AI (smartphone, IoT), Physical AI (automotive, robotics) and Cloud AI (data centre, networking). Rene made the load-bearing forecast: "we expect in a few years our data center business to be our largest business, larger than mobile."

**May 2026 (Q4 FY26): the pivot lands.** Arm announced the Arm AGI CPU — its own silicon, a physical product it sells, with Meta as lead partner. This is a different company. Arm now sells IP, subsystems, *and* chips. Management put hard numbers behind it: "more than $2 billion of customer demand across fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028... more than double what we stated at launch," on track to "$15 billion by fiscal '31," alongside an IP business management expects "to double to $10 billion."

**What was quietly dropped.** Two things. First, Armv9 penetration disclosure — a headline metric through FY25 — was retired in Q1 FY26 ("we're now just going to update this on an annual basis"), with Rene supplying a reason that is analytically true but conveniently timed: the one-to-one link between v9 adoption and royalty rate "should be separated out." A company stops disclosing a penetration metric when the metric is maturing. Second, and more quietly, the tariff/macro caveat that dominated the May 2025 and July 2025 calls simply evaporated by FY26 without ever being resolved — it was narrative weather, not analysis.

**The arc in one line:** a high-margin toll-collector on other people's chips became a company that also builds chips, and the market re-rated it as though the second business carries the economics of the first. It does not — management said so itself (see §2).

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

### The claim that fails: "royalty momentum"

Every version of the bull case rests on royalties — the recurring, near-costless per-chip toll that is the actual annuity. Management describes it as accelerating. The reported numbers say it decelerated hard in the most recent quarter.

| Quarter | Royalty revenue | YoY growth | Management's framing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q4 FY25 (May-25) | $607M | +18% | "record royalty" |
| Q1 FY26 (Jul-25) | $585M | +25% | "strong momentum across all end markets" |
| Q2 FY26 (Nov-25) | $620M | +21% | "record $620 million" |
| Q3 FY26 (Feb-26) | $737M | **+27%** | "Royalties increased 27% to a record $737 million" — *led the call with it* |
| Q4 FY26 (May-26) | **$671M** | **+11%** | "Royalty revenue grew 11%" — *stated third, after licensing* |

Two facts the narrative does not carry. Royalty growth **more than halved in one quarter, from 27% to 11%**. And in absolute dollars royalties **fell $66M sequentially**, from $737M to $671M — the annuity shrank. Some of that is ordinary smartphone seasonality. The growth-rate collapse is not seasonality; it is a comparison against the year-ago quarter, and it went from 27 to 11.

Watch where it sits in the script. In February, royalties led Rene's remarks. In May, licensing led and royalties came third. Management re-ordered the call around the number that looked better. That is a presentation choice, and it is the kind of choice that tends to precede a disclosure problem rather than follow one.

This also right-sizes the most-quoted bull statistic. "Data center royalty has more than doubled year-over-year" is true and is repeated on every call. But Jason Child sized that business himself in Q2 FY26: cloud and networking "ended the year at around 10-ish percent" of royalties, trending "somewhere in the 15% to 20% range." So the data-centre story is doubling a slice worth roughly a sixth of royalties, while the other ~80% — mobile, IoT — decelerates underneath it. Doubling 15% and stalling 85% produces exactly the +11% that was printed. **The bull case's best fact and the bear case's best fact are the same fact.**

### The claim that is partly self-dealt: "licensing momentum"

Reported Q4 FY26 licensing: $819M, +29% — the number that carried the quarter and the year. Then Jason Child disclosed this, unprompted, in the same paragraph:

> "Of the $819 million of license revenue, our agreement with SoftBank for technology licensing and design services contributed $200 million, flat with the prior quarter."

SoftBank is Arm's controlling shareholder. So **$200M — 24% of the quarter's licensing line — is revenue billed to the company's own parent**, at a $800M annualised run-rate against a $2.31B licensing business (~35%), and roughly 16% of total company revenue. Because it was "flat with the prior quarter," Q3 FY26 contained $200M as well: **at least $400M of FY26's $2.31B licensing is disclosed related-party revenue**, with further undisclosed amounts in Q1 and Q2 (both calls mention SoftBank agreements being "expanded" without giving a figure).

Strip the disclosed $200M out of Q4: third-party licensing was **$619M, against $634M reported in the year-ago quarter**. The year-ago figure may itself contain an undisclosed SoftBank amount, so treat this as indicative rather than exact — but the direction is unambiguous. **Reported licensing grew 29%; licensing from actual customers was flat to slightly down.** The growth in the line that carried the year came substantially from the parent.

This is not an accounting allegation. It is disclosed, it is legal, and design-services work for SoftBank may be perfectly genuine. But revenue from your own ~87%-owner is not evidence of market demand, it is not arm's-length price discovery, and it cannot be extrapolated. Every model that capitalises Arm's licensing growth as a market signal is capitalising, in part, an intercompany transfer — while the same controlling shareholder's founder publicly floats a "$4 trillion" valuation for the asset he controls (widely reported 2026-06-24). The party paying the revenue and the party talking the multiple are the same party.

### The claim that survives: growth, margins, delivery

To be fair to management, the top line is real and the quality of the franchise is not in question.

| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Third consecutive year of 20%+ growth" | FY24 $3.23B → FY25 $4.01B → FY26 $4.92B (+23%) | **True** |
| Best-in-class margins | Gross 92.5%, stable; net margin 18.4%; FCF margin 19.9% | **True** |
| Earnings inflecting | Net income $306M (FY24) → $792M (FY25) → $904M (FY26); non-GAAP EPS record $1.77 | **True** |
| No balance-sheet risk | Net **cash** $3.14B (cash $3.60B vs total debt $457M); Altman-Z 81 | **True** |
| Ecosystem scale | 22M developers (~80% of global base); 350B cumulative chips; ~50% share at top hyperscalers | **True, and the core of the moat** |

Note the returns, though. **ROIC 8.0% and ROE 11.3%** are pedestrian. Much of that is an artifact of goodwill from SoftBank's 2016 take-private sitting in invested capital, plus deliberate R&D suppressing current earnings — so I do not read low ROIC as a weak franchise. But it does mean the current 92.5% gross margin is not translating into high returns on the capital actually employed, and any model paying an extreme multiple is paying for the gross margin, not for the returns.

### The claim nobody has priced: the mix shift dilutes the model

This is the most under-discussed item in the file, and management supplied it themselves. Jason Child, Q4 FY26, on the economics of the new silicon business:

> "I think we said the IP business probably gets to something like a 65% operating margin business... and that the chip business is probably in the 35-ish percent range."

And Harlan Sur's question on the same call put first-generation chip **gross** margin at "about 30% plus," unchallenged.

So the $15B-by-FY31 silicon business that justifies the re-rating is a **30-35% gross-margin hardware business being bolted onto a 92.5% gross-margin IP business.** Growing revenue from $4.9B at 92.5% to $25B at a blended margin far below that is *more revenue and a structurally worse business model*. The market is applying an intellectual-property multiple to a revenue base that is deliberately mixing toward hardware. Growth and quality are moving in opposite directions here, and only one of them is in the multiple.

### The screener's valuation models

All five intrinsic methods (discounted cash flow, earnings power, Graham, owner earnings, IV15) return −100% margin of safety, and the DCF prints a $12.4 fair value. That specific number is nonsense — these models break on high-growth, high-multiple names and should not be quoted. But the *direction* is unanimous and worth one line: not one intrinsic method the system runs can reach the current price from current cash flows. At $262 the stock trades at roughly **293x trailing free cash flow, ~148x FY26 non-GAAP earnings, and ~56x enterprise value to sales.**

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising — to the point of becoming a warning signal.**

The confidence is not defensive; it is expanding, and it expands fastest exactly where evidence is thinnest.

- **May 2025 — hedged.** The most honest call in the set. Management declined full-year guidance outright: "we do not consider it prudent to issue full year guidance," citing "lower visibility than is traditional to start the year." Tariff exposure was quantified with real precision ("10% to 20% of our revenues stems from shipments into the US").
- **July 2025 — expanding.** "The AI revolution is accelerating and Arm is at its heart." First floating of chiplets/full solutions. Caveats still present but shrinking.
- **November 2025 — superlative.** "The future has never been brighter."
- **February 2026 — universal claims.** "Only Arm's compute platform can address these demands." "We believe every end application will run AI through Arm." Note that this call was conducted with the transcription mangling the company name into "Arm Holdings plc American Depositary Shares" throughout — a transcript artifact, not a management issue, and I have discounted it accordingly.
- **May 2026 — total.** "Customers want Arm at the center of the AI data center."

The trajectory is monotonic and it is unanchored. Between May 2025 ("we can't guide the year") and May 2026 ("$15 billion by fiscal '31"), **visibility did not improve — the forecast horizon extended from one quarter to five years.** A management team that could not see two quarters ahead in 2025 is now underwriting 2031. Nothing in the evidence explains what changed to make a five-year forecast possible; what changed is that the stock went from roughly $105 in January 2026 to $452.70 in June. Confidence expanded with the share price, not with information.

The one genuinely candid moment cuts the other way and is quoted in §5 — Rene's answer on the market's jitteriness ("we're in uncharted waters") was the most honest thing said in five calls.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium-High on delivery, with a compressing cushion that undercuts the headline.**

The 86% beat rate (6 of 7) is real. But *magnitude* is the whole story, and it is deteriorating:

| Report date | EPS actual | EPS estimate | Beat margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-11-06 | $0.10 | $0.25 | **−60% (miss)** |
| 2025-02-05 | $0.40 | $0.342 | +17.0% |
| 2025-05-07 | $0.55 | $0.525 | +4.8% |
| 2025-07-30 | $0.35 | $0.3491 | **+0.3%** |
| 2025-11-05 | $0.39 | $0.3287 | +18.6% |
| 2026-02-04 | $0.43 | $0.41 | +4.9% |
| 2026-05-06 | $0.60 | $0.58 | +3.4% |

The recent pattern — +4.8%, +0.3%, +4.9%, +3.4% — is a company landing inside its own guidance range, not sandbagging. Arm guides conservatively and clears the bar by a hair. That is honest management and a perfectly good operating record. It is also **thin cover for a stock priced at ~148x earnings**: at this multiple, a 3% beat is not a beat, it is a miss against the price. The one true miss (Nov 2024, −60%) shows what the downside gap looks like when it goes wrong.

Where management has been genuinely reliable: royalty guidance. They guided "mid-teens" royalty growth for Q2 FY26 and printed 21%. Where they hedge: licensing, always, and correctly — "licensing revenue varies quarter-to-quarter due to normal fluctuations in timing and size."

**The credibility item that matters most is management contradicting the bull case in plain language.** On licensing — the line carrying the story — Jason Child has now said the same thing on four consecutive calls, while reported ACV (annualised contract value, the smoothed run-rate of licensing deals) ran at 22-28%:

> Q4 FY25: "we've said in the past that we were typically looking to mid to high single-digit growth as being the right target. I think that's still the right target. ACV right now is running 15% because we've been overachieving very much due in part to AI."
> Q1 FY26: "We have not changed our long-term view of licensing growth of mid- to high single digits."
> Q2 FY26: ACV "well above... our long-term expectations of mid- to high single-digit growth."
> Q4 FY26: "the long-term target is probably in the high single-digit, low double-digit range... I would expect at least 10% year-on-year growth for the long term is probably the floor."

**Arm's own CFO has told the street four times that the licensing growth rate it is extrapolating is not sustainable, and named the structural rate: high single digits to low double digits.** He even names the cause — "this kind of AI investment super cycle or whatever folks are calling it... who knows how much longer it goes." This is not a bear taking a shot; it is the CFO refusing to underwrite his own reported numbers. Consensus capitalises 22-28%. Management guides ~10%.

That is the highest-integrity disclosure in this file, and it is the single most damaging fact for the bulls.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**Deflected: the specific content of the AI/Stargate opportunity.** Vijay Rakesh (Q4 FY25) asked directly what Stargate means for licence versus royalty. Jason: "that's all we're saying publicly Vijay." Twelve months later the same opacity persists — Stargate is cited as evidence ("5 new Stargate sites this quarter... expands visibility") without a single attached revenue figure. The named partnerships (Meta, OpenAI, Stargate, Cerebras) are announced as *validation*; none is sized. This is the recurring pattern: **logos in place of numbers.**

**Deflected: unannounced product strategy.** Lee Simpson (Q4 FY25) asked whether the chiplet work was "a waypoint perhaps to the eventual own chip-making Arm." Rene: "regarding unannounced products, I'm not going to announce anything here." **He was building exactly that, and it shipped as the Arm AGI CPU twelve months later.** Simpson identified the pivot four quarters before the announcement and management batted it away. The analyst was right; the disclosure was not. Nothing improper — but it means management's non-answers are informative, and should be read as such going forward.

**The question that later turned into the downgrade.** Harlan Sur (Q4 FY26) pressed on the chip business cost structure and Jason answered — then volunteered the hedge that now defines the bear case:

> "let's just assume that's the number until we work through some of the wafer and memory shortage issues."

**Management pre-flagged supply constraints on the AGI ramp on 2026-05-06.** On 2026-07-14 HSBC downgraded Arm to Hold on precisely that thesis — foundry capacity bottlenecks limiting earnings upside (while raising its target to $315 from $255) — and BofA the same day flagged near-term pain for Arm and Intel while favouring AMD. **The bear case is not an outside opinion; it is management's own caveat, which the market took ten weeks to price.**

**What analysts are not asking.** Three things, and their absence is conspicuous:
1. **Nobody asked about the $200M/quarter of SoftBank related-party revenue.** It was disclosed on 2026-05-06 and drew not one follow-up. The largest quality-of-earnings item in the business is uninterrogated.
2. **Nobody asked why royalty growth fell from 27% to 11%.** The annuity halved its growth rate and the Q&A went to core counts and memory technology.
3. **Nobody asked what the mix shift to 30-35% gross-margin silicon does to the multiple.** Sur asked about chip-business *cost structure*; nobody connected it to the blended margin or the valuation.

The Q&A has stopped being adversarial. Lee Simpson opened the Q4 FY26 call with "Well done everyone on a great quarter." When the sell side is congratulating rather than testing, the marginal buyer is buying the narrative, not the disclosure.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Milliwatts to megawatts" became "milliwatts to gigawatts."** Q1 FY26 through Q2 FY26 used megawatts; Q3 FY26 says gigawatts. A thousand-fold rhetorical escalation with no underlying change. Small, but it is the tell of a narrative inflating to match a multiple.

**The R&D justification arrives before the product.** Every call from Q1 FY26 forward contains a sentence explaining that today's costs buy tomorrow's revenue — "Arm's revenues today come from technology developed years or even decades ago, and our costs today are investments for future revenue streams." This is true, and it is also an unfalsifiable frame: it converts any margin compression into evidence of future growth. Watch it, because opex is stepping up again (see §8) and this sentence is what will be deployed to explain it.

**The Malaysia and Indonesia deals are the same trade, and it is not a chip trade.** Q4 FY25: "a multi-year AI partnership with the Malaysian government." Q4 FY26: "a long-term strategic partnership with the Indonesian government." Sovereign AI deals are lumpy, politically contingent, non-recurring, and land in the licensing line that the street extrapolates. Two data points is a pattern worth naming: some of Arm's "record licensing" is government cheques, not customer demand.

**Rene's single most honest moment.** Asked (Q3 FY26) about the market's treatment of software stocks, he broke frame: "we do see these kinds of things time to time where investors or the market gets jittery... we're in uncharted waters. And maybe that's why you're seeing some jittery numbers relative to how the market reacts." Buried inside it: "There's some AI going on there, but not nearly enough to be massively transformative yet... I think we're in super early days, to be quite frank." **The CEO's realistic view of AI adoption is materially more sober than his prepared remarks.** The scripted Arm says AI is everywhere; the unscripted Rene says enterprise AI has barely started. Both can be true — but only one is in the multiple.

**A new voice, briefly.** Q3 FY26 was hosted by Jessica Vall (Head of IR); Jeff Kvaal returned by Q4 FY26. Not material on its own — noted only because IR turnover around a strategy pivot is worth tracking rather than assuming.

**Nobody says "RISC-V."** Across five calls and roughly 25 analyst questions, the open-source instruction-set architecture that structurally threatens Arm's licensing model is never mentioned — not by management, not by a single analyst. Silence is not safety. It is the longest-dated risk in the story and it is entirely undiscussed.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

Not deteriorating — the franchise is strengthening on almost every operating axis. But this is unambiguously a pivot, and it must be classified as one: Arm has gone from selling designs to selling chips, funded by opex growing faster than revenue, with a five-year forecast attached to a business that did not exist eighteen months ago. Calling this "strengthening" would let the director size it as a compounder. It is a compounder *executing a category change* — and category changes are where good businesses are repriced.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:**

> **Every incremental dollar of Arm's forecast revenue is worth less than the dollars it already earns — and the multiple assumes the opposite.**

Unpack it, because it governs the sizing:
- The **royalty annuity** (92.5% gross margin, near-zero incremental cost) is the asset that deserves an extreme multiple. It grew **11%** last quarter, down from 27%.
- The **licensing line** (+25% in FY26) that is carrying the story contains at least $400M of disclosed FY26 revenue from the controlling shareholder at an $800M annual run-rate, plus sovereign government deals — and the CFO has said four times that its structural rate is ~10%, not 25%.
- The **AGI silicon business** driving the $15B FY31 target is a **30-35% gross-margin** hardware business — one-third the margin of the franchise it is being multiplied against — and management has already hedged its ramp on wafer and memory shortages.

So the mix is deteriorating even as the total grows, and the market is paying ~293x free cash flow, ~148x FY26 non-GAAP earnings and ~56x EV/sales for the blend. The immediate pressure point is **July 29, 2026** (Q1 FY27, after the close): consensus is **$0.40 EPS on $1.263B revenue** — that is **−33% in earnings and −15% in revenue sequentially** off Q4's $0.60/$1.49B, because the $819M licensing quarter does not repeat and because the CFO already told the street opex steps up "low double-digit sequential growth" into Q1. **An optically ugly quarter is contractually scheduled into a tape that just sold chip stocks off despite a TSMC blowout (2026-07-16).**

The director should size for the possibility that the pivot is *right* and the stock still falls, because the price already contains the pivot working.

### ECONOMIC MOAT

**Type: intangible-asset (the architecture itself) compounded by network effects and switching costs — the strongest structural combination available.** The Arm instruction set is the substrate ~80% of the world's developers build on; 22 million of them and 350 billion shipped chips mean the cost of leaving is not a licence fee, it is recompiling civilisation's software. Rene's flywheel description (Q1 FY26) is one of the rare pieces of management framing that is simply accurate.

**Width: WIDE. Trend: WIDENING.** The evidence supports this on the metrics that measure a moat rather than a cycle: gross margin 92.5% and *stable*; royalty **rate per chip rising every single generation** ("each generation of v9 is higher than the previous one... the royalty rates will continue to grow faster than v9 adoption," Q1 FY26); smartphone royalties growing "an order of magnitude faster than the market" while unit shipments grow ~2%; hyperscaler share ~50%; ~100% share in data-centre DPUs and SmartNICs; CSS attach rising with each generation at higher rates. **Pricing power that rises every generation, delivered against flat unit volumes, is the cleanest possible signature of a widening moat.**

I want to be explicit that **ROIC of 8.0% does not make this an eroding moat**, and the distinction matters. Eroding means high-but-*falling* returns and compressing margins. Arm's returns are *low but rising* (net income $306M → $792M → $904M across FY24-26 with margins expanding, gross margin flat at 92.5%). The low ROIC is a balance-sheet artifact of SoftBank's 2016 take-private goodwill sitting in invested capital plus deliberate R&D suppression — not competitive decay. The franchise is getting stronger, not weaker. **The problem with this stock is entirely the price, and not at all the moat.** Any bear case that argues erosion is arguing the wrong thing and will be wrong.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE — and Arm sits on the winning side of the one force reshaping its industry.** AI displacement is a tailwind here, not a risk: AI demands compute, compute demands power efficiency, and power efficiency is precisely Arm's franchise. Rene's argument is sound ("AI is not gonna replace a physical chip anytime soon").

The genuine long-term threat is **RISC-V** — the free, open-source instruction set that attacks the architecture-licensing model at its economic root. It is not a terminal threat today: Arm's ecosystem lead is measured in decades of compiled software and 22 million developers, and switching costs of that magnitude do not fall to a cheaper price. But it is the one force that could eventually commoditise the toll booth, and the fact that **neither management nor a single analyst uttered the word across five calls** tells you how thoroughly the market has stopped pricing it. Long-dated, live, and free of charge in the current multiple.

**Therefore: this is not a value trap, and it is not a fear-print.** It is the third thing — an outstanding, structurally widening franchise trading at a price that already discounts management's full five-year plan executed flawlessly. There is no cheapness here to diagnose. The terminal value is intact and growing; the entry price is the entire problem.
